title: Chapter 112: Wangxian: Forgetting Envy 2
content:
Chapter 112

Three months later. Guangling.

High on a hillside, a tight knot of villagers crept toward a patch of woods, brandishing torches in one hand and clutching farm tools as makeshift weapons in the other.

A desolate, neglected graveyard sat tucked into this ridge. For months, things had been far from quiet. Driven to their wits' end by the restless spirits terrorizing the foot of the hill, the locals had finally pooled their resources and hired a few wandering cultivators passing through town to root out the source once and for all.

Dusk was settling fast. The shrill hum of cicadas filled the air, and waist-high brambles rustled and whispered around them, as if unseen horrors were lying in wait to strike. Yet every time the men parted the weeds with trembling hands and swept their torches through the dark, it turned out to be nothing more than a false alarm.

Swords drawn, the cultivators led the jittery villagers through the overgrown meadow and deeper into the treeline.

The wild graveyard spread out beneath the canopy. Crooked slabs of weather-beaten stone and splintered wooden markers leaned at gruesome angles, swallowed by a bone-chilling, bitter wind. The cultivators exchanged brief glances and drew their paper talismans, preparing for a routine cleansing. Seeing how calm and collected their hirelings were, several villagers let out quiet sighs of relief—it couldn't be that bad.

That sigh caught right in their throats.

With a sickening, heavysmack, a gory, mangled corpse slammed down onto a nearby burial mound.

The villager closest to the heap let out a blood-curdling shriek, dropping his torch and scrambling backward on all fours. A heartbeat later, a second mangled body crashed down. Then a third. A fourth. Freshly butchered corpses began pelting the forest floor like a torrential downpour of rotting meat. Chaos erupted in an instant, terrified wails tearing through the woods.

The young cultivators had never witnessed anything remotely this grotesque, but they clung desperately to their bravado. Their leader barked, "Hold your ground! Do not panic! It’s nothing more than a minor haunting—"

The words died in his throat, cut off as if an iron hand had clamped down on his windpipe.

His gaze had snagged on a tall tree.

Perched comfortably on a high branch was a lone figure in pitch-black robes. A single, slender black boot dangled over the edge, swinging lazily to and fro with breezy, infuriating nonchalance.

Tucked into his sash was an ink-black flute, its blood-red tassel swaying in rhythm with his kicking leg.

The cultivators went ash-white.

The villagers had just begun to swallow down their panic at the squad leader's commanding shout—only to watch all of the cultivators turn deathly pale, spin on their heels, and bolt. The cultivators tore out of the woods like a howling gale, vanishing down the slope without a backward glance and leaving the townsfolk entirely to their fate. Realizing that whatever horror nested on this hill was so apocalyptic even the immortals fled from it, the villagers lost their minds. Scattering like birds before a hawk, they broke into a dead sprint.

One straggler tripped over his own boots, taking a hard dive and mouthful of dirt. Thinking he was good as dead, he looked up—and his eyes caught the sudden, radiant gleam of a young man in pristine white robes standing just ahead.

A long sword rested at the stranger’s hip, and a soft, ethereal aura seemed to shimmer across his skin, cutting through the murky forest like a celestial being who had stepped out of the clouds.

Scrambling toward him, the villager blurted in a frantic gasp, "Gongzi! Kind gongzi, save me! There are ghosts—hurry, strike down that mon—"

Before the plea could clear his mouth, another dripping corpse slammed flat onto the earth right between them. The blood-caked face, oozing black rot from every orifice, stared directly into his eyes at point-blank range.

Just as the poor man was about to pass out from sheer terror, the white-robed man dropped a single, level syllable:

"Leave."

It was only one word, but a wave of profound, inexplicable relief washed over the villager, carrying the absolute authority of an imperial pardon. A surge of frantic adrenaline shot through his limbs; he scrambled to his feet and ran like hell without daring to look back.

The white-robed newcomer swept a quiet, assessing glance over the blood-soaked corpses dragging themselves aimlessly through the underbrush, seemingly at a loss for how to even catalog the mess. He tilted his chin upward.

Up in the canopy, the dark-robed rogue dropped down as light as a fallen leaf. In a breath, he flashed into the man's personal space, pinning him firmly against a broad tree trunk.

A teasing murmur brushed against his ear: "Well, well. If it isn't the pure and untouchable Hanguang-jun, Lan Wangji. What brings you wandering onto my turf?"

All around them, mutilated bloody ghouls crawled blindly and ferociously through the dirt. The rogue planted a single hand against the bark beside his ear, trapping Lan Wangji flush between his chest and the timber.

Lan Wangji’s expression remained stone-still.

The rogue flashed a grin. "Since you were kind enough to deliver yourself to my doorstep, don't mind if I—whoa, hey!"

Lan Wangji’s grip snapped around both of his wrists, locking them tight with a single hand.

Tables turned in half a breath. Trapped neatly under the counter-pin, the rogue gasped in over-the-top dramatics: "Good heavens, Hanguang-jun! The raw power! Unbelievable, staggering, truly shocking! Subduing me with only one hand—I'm utterly defenseless! What a terrifying man!"

Lan Wangji said nothing.

His knuckles tightened their grip.

Instantly, the rogue's awe twisted into theatrical terror. "Ah, mercy, it hurts! Spare me, Hanguang-jun, I’ll never do it again! Please don't hold me so tight—and whatever you do, don't tie me up! Definitely don't pin me to the dirt, whatever you do—"

Watching him lay the shameless, ridiculous act on thicker by the second, Lan Wangji’s brow gave a faint, long-suffering twitch. He finally cut him off: "...Enough fooling around."

Wei Wuxian was having far too much fun begging for mercy. He blinked innocently. "Why? I haven't even finished pleading for my life yet."

Lan Wangji muttered flatly, "You plead for your life every single day. Stop playing around."

Wei Wuxian leaned in close, his voice dropping to a feather-light purr. "Didn't you demand it yourself? Every day means every day."

He pressed in impossibly close, hovering as if about to steal a kiss, yet stubbornly refused to close the final fraction of an inch. Their lips drifted together and apart, separated by nothing more than the breath between them—like a fickle, mischievous butterfly fluttering over the petals of a poised blossom, brushing against it without ever landing.

Under that relentless teasing, a crack broke through Lan Wangji's cool exterior; his pale amber eyes flickered, his jaw tightening as the stoic blossom finally leaned forward of its own accord to catch the wayward wing.

Wei Wuxian tipped his chin up on a dime, dodging the kiss cleanly.

He arched an eyebrow. "Call me gege."

Lan Wangji stared back, stony-faced.

"Call me gege," Wei Wuxian coaxed, a wicked smirk playing on his lips. "Call me that, and you get a kiss."

Lan Wangji’s lips parted, twitching faintly.

In all his life, he had never once let that cloyingly sweet, affectionate term cross his tongue. Even with Lan Xichen, he strictly used the formal, uprightxiongzhang.

Wei Wuxian leaned on the pressure, soft and wheedling: "Just once, let me hear it. Think of how many times I’ve called you that! You call me that, we kiss, and who knows what comes next..."

Even if Lan Wangji had been on the verge of giving in, that brazen, suggestive jab completely did him in. The words dissolved behind his teeth, stubbornly choked back down. After a stiff pause, he hissed out two tight, flustered syllables: "...Shameless!"

Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Doesn't your arm get tired holding me with just one hand? Having only one hand free makes things so inconvenient, doesn't it?"

Gathering his composure, Lan Wangji asked with deadpan, icy formality, "And pray tell, what would you suggest I do?"

"Oh, let me teach you," Wei Wuxian chirped. "Why not just untie that forehead ribbon of yours and bind my wrists together? Much easier that way."

Lan Wangji held the grinning rogue’s gaze in heavy silence for a moment. Slowly, deliberately, he reached up, slid the white ribbon from his brow, and drew the silk taut before Wei Wuxian's eyes.

Then, with blinding, ruthless speed, he lashed the ribbon around Wei Wuxian’s wrists, pinning his wayward hands securely above his head against the tree trunk, before burying his face straight into the crook of his neck.

A sudden, sharp shriek cut through the brush.

The two separated instantly. Lan Wangji’s hand snapped to the hilt of Bichen, but he held his blade in check—the cry had been high, crisp, and distinctly that of a young child. Striking blindly ran the risk of hurting an innocent passerby.

The waist-high grass rustled violently as a small, frantic figure scrambled away through the weeds. Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji tracked the trail a few paces downhill until a woman's breathless, ecstatic cry drifted up the slope:

"Mianmian! Are you alright?! What were you thinking, running off in a place like this? You scared your mother half to death!"

Wei Wuxian froze. "Mianmian?"

The name was intimately familiar, scratching at the back of his mind, when a man’s voice joined in, stern and laced with panic: "I told you not to wander off while we're night-hunting! You just charged ahead on your own—if some ghoul had dragged you into a ditch, what were your mother and I supposed to do?! ...Mianmian? What’s wrong? Why are you looking like that?"

He turned his focus toward his wife, his tone turning fretful. "Qingyang, check her over, quick! Did something happen to her? Why does she look so shaken up? Did she run into something she shouldn't have seen up there?"

...Well, she had definitely seen something she shouldn't have seen.

Lan Wangji cut a sharp, dry look sideways at Wei Wuxian.

Wei Wuxian met his gaze with wide, puppy-dog eyes, mouthing in pure, unrepentant innocence:Oh, what a sin.

Seeing that the man didn't possess a single shred of remorse for corrupting a minor, Lan Wangji gave an exasperated shake of his head. The two stepped out from the ruined cemetery and rounded the crest of the hill.

Down the slope, three figures snapped their heads toward them, instantly stiffening with guarded suspicion. The man and woman were clearly husband and wife, crouching in the weeds beside a little girl of about ten with twin topknots. The woman was slender and pretty, carrying a spiritual sword at her waist; the moment her eyes caught Wei Wuxian, the steel cleared its scabbard with a hiss, the tip leveled straight at his chest.

"Who goes there?!" she barked.

Wei Wuxian raised his hands, breezy as ever. "Whoever we are, we're living, breathing people. Nothing to lose sleep over."

She opened her mouth to snap back, but her eyes slid past his shoulder to the man trailing behind him. She froze mid-breath. "Hanguang-jun?"

Lan Wangji was standing there without his forehead ribbon; for a second, she genuinely doubted her own eyes. If not for that impossibly striking, unforgettable face, she would have dismissed it as a hallucination. Her gaze flickered back to Wei Wuxian, dazed realization dawning in her eyes. "Then... then you... you're..."

The Yiling Laozu’s return had been the talk of the entire cultivation world for months. The man standing shoulder-to-shoulder with Lan Wangji could only be one person. Taking in the sudden, trembling excitement washing over her face, paired with the faint prick of familiarity in her features, Wei Wuxian’s mind spun:Wait, does this lady know me? Did we have beef? Did I flirt with her back in the day? No, I definitely don't remember any girl named Qingyang... Wait. Mianmian!

Light dawned on his face. "You're Mianmian?!"

Her husband’s eyes flared, bristling defensively. "What're you yelling my daughter's name for?!"

It turned out the adventurous little girl who had accidentally walked in on them was Mianmian’s daughter, named after her mother. Wei Wuxian was thoroughly charmed.Well, look at that. Big Mianmian and Little Mianmian.

Lan Wangji dipped his head in a formal, respectful bow. "Luo-guniang."

Tucking a stray strand of hair behind her ear, she returned the courtesy with a soft dip. "Hanguang-jun." Turning to Wei Wuxian, she added, "Wei-gongzi."

Wei Wuxian offered her a warm, easy grin. "Luo-guniang. Ah, I finally know your actual name after all these years."

Luo Qingyang flushed with bashful amusement, a little sheepish at the sudden reminder of ancient teenage antics. She gently pulled her husband forward. "This is my husband."

Seeing that the two strangers carried no malice, the man’s stiff posture relaxed. After a polite exchange of pleasantries, Wei Wuxian asked offhandedly, "Which sect do you hail from, sir?"

The man answered frankly, with a bright smile: "None of them, I'm afraid."

Luo Qingyang looked at her partner, her eyes soft with affection. "My husband isn't a cultivator. He used to be a merchant. But... he's willing to accompany me on night-hunts."

For an ordinary mortal man to willingly walk away from a safe, comfortable life—embracing a rootless, itinerant existence without flinching at danger, just to roam the dangerous fringes of the realm with his wife—was a rare, precious thing. Wei Wuxian felt a wave of genuine, quiet respect swell in his chest.

"You're here for the haunting as well?" Wei Wuxian asked.

Luo Qingyang nodded. "We are. Word reached us that restless spirits in this hillside graveyard were running amok, making life a misery for the local villagers. We came by to see if we could lend a hand. Have the two of you already handled it?"

If Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji had stepped in, there was zero need for anyone else to get involved.

Wei Wuxian shook his head. "Those villagers fed you a line."

Luo Qingyang blinked. "How so?"

"They claim the spirits attacked unprovoked, but the truth is, the villagers dug up the graves themselves to plunder the burial goods, tossing the bones into the dirt like garbage. The dead were simply returning the favor."

Her husband frowned in confusion. "Is that right? But even so, surely a haunting didn't justify taking several human lives?"

Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji traded a glance. "That was fabricated too," Wei Wuxian said. "Nobody died. We looked into it—a few grave-robbers got the daylights scared out of them by vengeful ghosts and took to their beds for a couple of weeks, and one idiot shattered his leg sprinting down the hill in a panic. Aside from that, zero casualties. The 'multiple deaths' were pure sensationalist garbage cooked up to bait stronger cultivators into cleaning up their mess."

The husband was floored. "Truly? How utterly shameless!"

Luo Qingyang let out a heavy sigh. "People... they never change." She paused, as if dragged under by an old memory, giving a quiet shake of her head. "It's the same everywhere you go."

Wei Wuxian shrugged. "Well, I gave them a proper scare just now. After tonight, they won't dare touch those graves again, which means the dead won't have any reason to bother them. Problem solved."

"What if they hire another sect to force a purge?" she asked.

Wei Wuxian flashed a wicked smirk. "I showed my face."

Understanding flashed across her features. Once those trembling hirelings spread the word that the Yiling Laozu had personally marked this territory as his own, which cultivator would be suicidal enough to march up this hill looking for trouble?

Luo Qingyang laughed softly. "I see. When Mianmian came barreling back down looking like she’d seen a demon, I feared she’d run into a horrific evil spirit. If she was rude to you, please don't take it to heart."

Wei Wuxian thought privately:No, no, pretty sure we were the ones putting on a wildly inappropriate show.

Outwardly, he maintained absolute, solemn composure: "Not at all, not at all. We gave Little Mianmian quite a fright—we should be the ones apologizing."

Her husband scooped the little girl into his arms. Perched securely against her father's chest, Mianmian puffed her cheeks, glaring daggers at Wei Wuxian with a look of pure, mortified outrage that she couldn't possibly articulate. Dressed in a delicate pink frock, she had pale, snow-soft cheeks and dark, grape-like eyes; she was so adorable Wei Wuxian practically burned to pinch her face. Mindful of the doting father hovering right beside her, he settled for giving one of her bouncing topknots a gentle tug.

Hands tucked behind his back, he beamed at her. "Mianmian looks the spitting image of you when you were young, Luo-guniang."

Lan Wangji cast a quiet sideways glance at him, keeping his thoughts to himself.

Luo Qingyang chuckled, pressing a sleeve to her lips. "Wei-gongzi, do you feel no shame saying that with a straight face? As if you actually remember what I looked like as a child!"

That shy, pursed smile was an exact echo of the spirited girl in soft crimson silks from all those years ago. Wei Wuxian didn't have an ounce of embarrassment in his body. "Of course I remember! You haven't changed a bit. By the way, how old is she? Let me give her some warding-money."

Both parents hastily waved their hands. "No, no, that's really not necessary!"

"Nonsense, of course it is," Wei Wuxian laughed. "Not like it's coming out of my pocket anyway!"

Before the couple could process the quip, Lan Wangji’s hand had already drifted over, quietly placing a small handful of heavy silver coins into Wei Wuxian’s palm. Taking the shining tokens, Wei Wuxian insisted on tucking them into the little girl's hands. Seeing there was no refusing them, Luo Qingyang nudged her daughter. "Mianmian, thank Hanguang-jun and Wei-gongzi."

The little girl mumbled, "Thank you, Hanguang-jun."

Wei Wuxian pouted playfully. "Hey, Little Mianmian, I’m the one who handed them to you! Where’s my thank-you?"

Mianmian shot him a furious glare, refusing to utter a single syllable no matter how much he coaxed her. Instead, she ducked her head, tugging a red cord from beneath her collar to pull out an exquisite little embroidered sachet, jealously tucking the silver coins safely inside.

Having reached the foot of the hill, Wei Wuxian bade them a slightly wistful farewell, turning down a different path with Lan Wangji.

Once the pair had vanished around the bend, Luo Qingyang gently chided her daughter: "Mianmian. That was terribly rude. That man saved your mother’s life once."

Her husband’s eyes went wide. "Really?! Mianmian, you hear that? Look at how bad your manners were!"

The little girl buried her face in her father's collar, grumbling under her breath, "I... I don't like him."

Luo Qingyang teased, "You little rascal. If you truly disliked him, you would’ve chucked that silver right into the dirt."

Mianmian’s flushed little face pressed deeper into her father's chest, whining obstinately: "He was doing bad things!"

Luo Qingyang couldn't help a fond laugh. Before she could probe further, her husband asked curiously, "Qingyang, I remember you mentioning this Hanguang-jun before—you said he was a legendary figure from a renowned great sect. Why would someone of his standing show up in the middle of nowhere to hunt such minor spirits?"

Luo Qingyang explained with patient warmth, "Hanguang-jun isn't like other prominent cultivators. He has always gone wherever chaos calls. As long as restless spirits cause harm to the common folk, he will travel to their aid—regardless of how petty the creature is, or how little glory it brings."

Her husband nodded, admiration coloring his tone. "A true gentleman, then." He paused, his curiosity turning slightly anxious. "And that Wei-gongzi? You said he saved your life, but I don't recall you ever mentioning him. Did you find yourself in mortal danger back then?!"

Scooping Mianmian into her arms, a soft, radiant light flickered in Luo Qingyang’s eyes. She smiled gently. "Well, that Wei-gongzi..."

Down the other road, Wei Wuxian remarked to Lan Wangji, "To think that little girl from back then has a daughter of her own now!"

"Mn."

"Though it's hardly fair," Wei Wuxian grumbled, kicking a loose pebble. "Technically speaking, she walked in onyoudoing bad things tome. Why did she look at me like I was the villain?"

Before Lan Wangji could answer, Wei Wuxian spun on his heel, walking backward to face him. "Oh, I get it. Deep down, she definitely likes me. Just like a certain someone used to."

Lan Wangji brushed an invisible speck of dust from his sleeve, his tone cool and unbothered: "Return my forehead ribbon, Wei Yuandao."

Hearing the unfamiliar alias, Wei Wuxian blinked in confusion, took a beat to process it, and burst into a wicked snicker. "Look at you, Second Young Master Lan! Smells like someone’s drowning in jealousy!"

Lan Wangji’s lashes dipped low.

Wei Wuxian stepped right into his path, one arm hooking casually around his waist while the other cupped his chin, raising his face with exaggerated solemnity. "Come on, out with it. How many years have you been nursing this jar of jealousy? You hid it so well I couldn't even catch a whiff of it."

Used to his antics, Lan Wangji let his chin be tilted upward—only to feel a sly, wandering hand slip straight into his lapels.

Looking down, Wei Wuxian had already pulled his hand back, clutching an embroidered silk pouch with mock astonishment: "Well, well! What do we have here?"

It was Lan Wangji’s coin pouch.

Wei Wuxian twirled the delicate silk purse by its cords on his index finger, pointing an accusatory thumb at him. "Hanguang-jun, oh Hanguang-jun! Taking without asking is called stealing! What did the world call you back in the day? Scion of a noble house? Paragon of the gentry? Quite the paragon you are—quietly stewing in jealousy in the shadows, stealing the perfume sachet a pretty maiden gave me, and turning it into your personal coin purse! No wonder I couldn't find it anywhere after I woke up. If Little Mianmian hadn't been wearing the exact same sachet around her neck, I would've never remembered! Tsk, tsk. Come on, spill: how did you swipe it off me while I was unconscious? How long did you spend fondling me to find it?"

A faint ripple broke across Lan Wangji’s stoic features. He reached out to snatch it back, but Wei Wuxian tossed the pouch into the air, caught it with his other hand, and danced two steps backward out of reach.

"Resorting to force because you lost the argument? What's there to be shy about? Being bashful over this... now I finally understand why I'm so shameless! We really are a match made in heaven—all my shame must've been handed off to you, kept safe in your pocket."

A delicate dusting of pink dusted the shell of Lan Wangji’s ear, but his face remained taut as steel. His hand darted forward with blinding speed, but Wei Wuxian was faster on his feet, staying an inch out of reach like a phantom.

"You used to shove your purse into my robes willingly, so why're you getting stingy now?" Wei Wuxian teased, grinning from ear to ear. "Look at you—stealing keepsakes, stealing kisses, and going back on your word. Rotten straight to the core!"

Lan Wangji closed the distance in a single stride, finally wrapping his arms around him and locking him securely against his chest.

"We performed the bows," Lan Wangji murmured in quiet, earnest defense. "We are already... husbands. It is not stolen affection."

Wei Wuxian leaned into the embrace, laughing softly. "Even between husbands, you can't go muscling me around all the time! You always make me beg, and even when I do, you never stop. If your ancestors in the Cloud Recesses saw what you've become, they’d die of pure rage..."

Pushed past his limits, Lan Wangji silenced that clever, wicked mouth with a bruising, desperate kiss.

Translator's Notes:

[A/N 1] Warding-money (压祟钱 / yāsuìqián):A traditional Chinese custom where elders gift money to children during the new year or upon visits, originally intended as an amulet to suppress evil spirits and ward off misfortune (playing on the homophonesuifor 'demon/bad luck').

[A/N 2] Wei Yuandao (魏远道):Back during their youth at the Xuanwu cave, Wei Wuxian flirted with Mianmian by teasing her real name (Luo Qingyang) and cheekily claiming his name was "Wei Yuandao," reciting an ancient romantic poem:"Green, green grows the river grass; longing extends along the distant road (yuandao)."Lan Wangji bringing this up years later is his hilariously deadpan way of letting Wei Wuxian know he's been petty and jealous about that specific flirtation for over a decade.
